claims.claim: The 2019 guide (v1.08a) rests on the Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition and Merriam-Webster's Collegiate 11th edition, and covers only D&D-specific departures from them.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Merriam-Webster’s Collegiate Dictionary, 11th edition

claims.claim: The general rules bind every D&D product, not just rulebooks.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: whether RPG books, board games, novels, or something else

claims.claim: Editions are spelled out and lowercased ('fifth edition'), with 4E/5E abbreviations confined to tables, conversion documents, or informal text.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We write “fifth edition,” for instance, not “5th Edition.”

claims.claim: Writers are told not to rely on internet searches, wikis, or prior-edition products for setting facts.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Don’t rely on Internet searches

claims.claim: Tone is gated by a Lord of the Rings / Game of Thrones plausibility test; humor and tragedy are allowed only if they do not overtake the general tone.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: ring wraiths aren’t used for gags

claims.claim: D&D's brand voice frames adventure as a team's story rather than a lone knight's.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Teamwork and friendship are a huge part

claims.claim: Gender-neutral wording is expected whenever a person's gender is unknown or irrelevant, and the reader's gender is not assumed.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: gender neutrality whenever the gender of a person is unknown

claims.claim: Rules text achieves gender neutrality chiefly by being written in the second person.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: writing in the second person whenever possible

claims.claim: v1.08a newly permits singular 'they/their' but tells writers to reach for it only when no other pleasing alternative exists.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: but don’t abuse this liberty

claims.claim: 'He or she' is to be used sparingly; 'he/she' and 's/he' are banned; alternating he and she for inclusivity is banned.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: avoid “he/she” and “s/he” altogether

claims.claim: In 2019 'man' and 'woman' were reserved for humans only, so a dwarf is a 'male dwarf', never a 'dwarf man'.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: we write “male dwarf,” not “dwarf man”

claims.claim: Editorial rules such as the man/woman restriction may be broken in dialogue and first-person narrative, because a character need not follow house style.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: This rule can be broken in dialogue and first-person narrative

claims.claim: Gendered suffixes are avoided ('priest', 'actor'); 'priestess'/'actress' survive only inside an in-world title or organization name.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Avoid gender-specific suffixes whenever possible

claims.claim: Deities are called 'god' regardless of gender in editorial voice; 'goddess' is reserved for in-world usage.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: use “god” whether the deity is male or female

claims.claim: Headings descend Chapter Title > Heading 1 > 2 > 3 > Inline Subhead without skipping, and exist for structure, never aesthetics.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Use a heading for a structural reason, not an aesthetic one

claims.claim: The inline subhead (heading 4) is set in bold italics and ends with a period, exclamation point, or question mark, not a colon.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: should be followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon

claims.claim: Bold is the only emphasis device, and a term already in the section heading gets no emphasis in running text.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Use bold for such emphasis

claims.claim: Sidebars are rationed; any sidebar that must follow a specific passage to make sense should be folded into body text instead.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: The best sidebars can appear anywhere on a page

claims.claim: American spelling and punctuation are house style, with Merriam-Webster's first-listed variant winning (toward, backward).
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: we use “toward,” not “towards,”

claims.claim: The serial (Oxford) comma is mandatory.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We require the serial comma

claims.claim: Negative contractions (don't, can't, wasn't) are encouraged; other contractions are used with care where they could be misread.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We encourage the use of contractions formed with “not,”

claims.claim: 'Non-' is hyphenated before fantasy races (non-elf, non-drow) but closed for 'nonhuman', and numeral-plus-abbreviation compounds are never hyphenated (100 gp treasure).
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: non-elf, non-dwarf

claims.claim: Possessives follow Chicago 17th edition (7.16–29), including names ending in an unpronounced s.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We follow the approach in the seventeenth edition

claims.feature: words used as words / foreign words
claims.claim: English words used as words go in quotation marks; a non-English word, real or invented, is italicized when used as a word.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: is italicized when used as a word

claims.claim: Vertical lists are introduced by a complete sentence ending in a colon, items start with a capital, and closing punctuation appears only if items are full sentences.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: introduce it with a complete sentence ending with a colon

claims.claim: Whole numbers zero through one hundred are spelled out in prose (Chicago 9.2), with the usual exceptions for units, parts of a book, dates, and times.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: we spell out whole numbers from zero to one hundred

claims.claim: 'Percent' is written as a word except in tables or tight lists; percentile dice are 'd100', never 'd%'.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Use the word “percent,” rather than the symbol %

claims.claim: Cross-references are used judiciously; chapters are cited by number, subsections and sidebars by quoted title, tables by unquoted title.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Use cross-references judiciously

claims.claim: Appendices are lettered, not numbered, and cited like chapters ('see appendix A').
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We use letters, not numbers, for appendices

claims.claim: Page references are avoided because they are hand-added at galley and break across reprints; cross-product page references are especially discouraged.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We avoid page references as much as possible

claims.claim: In D&D fiction, thoughts and psionic speech may be set in italics, quotes, or plain type at the author's discretion, a reversal of the older policy.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Aesthetics and clarity should dictate appropriate usage

claims.claim: A character is 'on' a plane of existence but 'in' a plane named without the word 'plane' (in Elysium).
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: “She is in Elysium.”

claims.claim: Ability scores, action names, class features, feats, skills, languages, planes, and race/monster traits are capitalized as proper game terms.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Action names {the Attack action, the Dash action}

claims.claim: Spells, magic items, and artifacts are italicized and treated as titles, and the effect a spell creates is not italicized.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Spells {magic missile}

claims.claim: A stat block name is bolded in running text only at its first appearance in an encounter area, and nothing may sit between the number and the name.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: write “four goblins,” not “four loud goblins”

claims.claim: Rules prose uses numerals for points, damage, durations of game effects, and tactical distances, but spells out narrative quantities (six hours, fifty miles).
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: The two cities are fifty miles apart.

claims.claim: The guide fixes verb-noun pairings: you cast a spell, take damage, make a saving throw, finish a rest, score a critical hit.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: You take damage.

claims.claim: Rules must say 'succeed on a DC 15 check', not 'make a DC 15 check', unless the outcomes follow immediately.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: “You must succeed on a DC 15 Strength check

claims.claim: 'Save' for 'saving throw' is used sparingly, mainly in stat blocks; the 4E sense of 'save' as a successful saving throw is abandoned.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: use it sparingly, preferably only in a stat block

claims.claim: 'Result' no longer means the number on the die; it means the die roll plus modifiers, and 'total' is often preferred.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We often prefer the word “total”

claims.claim: 'Magic' is the adjective for objects (magic item, magic sword); 'magical' for other things; 'magical item' is forbidden.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: “magic item” and its variants should never be “magical item.”

claims.claim: Damage is written as '10 fire damage', never '10 points of fire damage'.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Avoid referring to points of damage

claims.claim: The die expression stays with the damage type: 'an extra 1d4 fire damage'.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We write “an extra 1d4 fire damage,”

claims.claim: One is proficient 'in' a skill, language, or activity but 'with' a tool, weapon, or armor.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: proficient in Elvish and Arcana

claims.claim: 'Dungeon Master' is never a verb except in conversational web writing.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: This term is a noun, not a verb

claims.feature: weeks and months banned in rules
claims.claim: Because week and month lengths vary by world (a Realms week is a tenday), rules durations are given in days or years, never weeks or months.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: say a game effect lasts for 7 days, not 1 week

claims.claim: 'Human' is not a synonym for 'mortal', and 'humanoid' is used cautiously because it names a creature type.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Beware of using “human” as a synonym for “mortal.”

claims.claim: A word list fixes spellings and plurals: dwarves not dwarfs, mithral not mithril, staffs, war band, drow/kenku/yuan-ti unchanged in plural.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: mithral (not mithril)

claims.feature: Forgotten Realms terms in the general guide
claims.claim: The general guide carries a short Realms list: Goodman/Goodwoman capped, 'goodsir' lowercased, 'godsforsaken' as the Realms form of godforsaken, and 'the Realms' only after 'the Forgotten Realms'.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: goodsir (a form of address, not capped)

claims.claim: 'Godsforsaken' is the established Realms form but is not required in other polytheistic settings, since 'godforsaken' has no necessary monotheistic sense.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: godsforsaken (established in the Realms

claims.claim: 'Fellowship' is avoided for a party because of its Tolkien association and because D&D parties are often fractious or mercenary; 'party', 'group', 'band', or 'company' are preferred.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: use “group,” “band,” “company,” or, especially, “party.”

claims.claim: Standard abbreviations are fixed (PH, DMG, MM, gp, d100, AC, DC, DM, XP, HD, hp, NPC).
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: NPC nonplayer character

claims.claim: The superseded 2013 guide banned singular they outside informal contexts like dialogue.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (2013)
claims.quote: Don’t use “they” or “their” as singular pronouns

claims.claim: The 2013 guide framed gender neutrality as assuming a readership of both men and women, a framing dropped in 2019 for 'we don't assume a gender identity'.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (2013)
claims.quote: readership includes both men and women

claims.claim: Sections absent from v1.04a and present in v1.08a include Gender-Specific Suffixes, Headings, Sidebars, Bulleted Lists, Appendix References, and Adventuring Parties (verified by heading presence in both texts).
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (2013)

claims.feature: existence of a post-2019 house style guide
claims.claim: A Word version of the house style guide, authored by Kim Mohan and last modified by Judy Bauer on 2021-07-06 at Wizards of the Coast, ships inside the Dungeoncraft Pack (2023-12-04) and postdates the public v1.08a PDF.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04

claims.claim: The 2021 docx cites merriam-webster.com rather than the printed 11th edition Collegiate.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: merriam-webster.com

claims.claim: The 2021 docx reverses the 2019 rule: 'man' and 'woman' may now describe the gender of any people, so 'dwarf man' and 'gnome woman' are fine.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: we can write “dwarf man” or “gnome woman.”

claims.claim: The 2021 docx allows they/their/them/themself for a person of unknown gender without the 2019 'don't abuse this liberty' caveat, requiring only a clear antecedent.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: you must ensure that the pronoun’s antecedent is clear

claims.claim: In running text a person's preferred pronoun (he, she, or they) is used; in rules text 'it' is used.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: In rules text, use “it.”

claims.claim: Descriptive text uses they/them for Humanoids and other sapient creatures of unknown gender (including vampires), and 'it' for animals, cosmic horrors, and extraplanar creatures.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: A beholder never keeps its promises.

claims.claim: Where 'they' would be ambiguous the sentence is reworded to avoid pronouns, e.g. by switching to the plural.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: reword to avoid using pronouns

claims.feature: 'it' for dehumanizing effect is an exception
claims.claim: Using 'it' for a sapient monster to emphasize inhumanity is allowed only as a rare deliberate effect.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Such exceptions should be rare.

claims.claim: Established characters keep their canonical pronouns regardless of species or type (Baphomet and Strahd he/him; Lolth and Tasha she/her).
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: He/Him: Baphomet, Strahd

claims.claim: The 2021 docx adds creature types (Humanoid, Fey, Undead) to the capitalized game terms, a convention the 2019 PDF lacks.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Creature type (Humanoid, Fey, Undead)

claims.claim: Bold stat-block names are explained functionally: bold signals that the term is a game object to be looked up, so 'Strahd likes to make vampire spawn' stays roman.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: this indicates the term is a game object

claims.claim: Effects triggered by hitting must say 'attack roll', because readers read 'attack' in its English sense and think fireball 'hits'.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: The word “attack” confuses many of our readers

claims.claim: 'Within X feet' literally reaches through total cover, so writers must add a sight/hearing/cover condition or use an official area of effect.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: use one of our official areas of effect

claims.claim: The box of game information is called a stat block; 'statistics' is reserved for the crunch in the abstract.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: call it a stat block

claims.claim: Lists, spells, and bestiary stat blocks are ordered letter-by-letter, ignoring spaces, with a warning that Word sorts word-by-word.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: We use letter-by-letter alphabetization.

claims.claim: The 2021 word list adds aasimar, blood red (contra Merriam-Webster), cyclopes, gold vs golden, insectile not insectoid, parlay vs parley, tabaxi, tenant vs tenet.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: insectile (not insectoid)

claims.feature: lowercase 'hit points' persists in the 2021 docx
claims.claim: The 2021 docx still writes 'hit points' lowercase in its examples, whereas the 2024 rules glossary capitalizes 'Hit Points', so even the internal 2021 guide predates 2024 house style.
claims.source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Anyone who touches the orb regains 3 hit points.

claims.claim: The AL adventure format prescribes boxed text only for a particularly important event, never for rooms or normalcy.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Boxed text should be used very sparingly

claims.claim: Boxed text is capped at one or two brief descriptive sentences.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: no more than one or two brief and descriptive sentences

claims.claim: Boxed text narrates exciting events only; the substance of an encounter lives under the headings beneath it.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: only provide a narrative for exciting events

claims.claim: The template's own sample boxed text is two descriptive sentences plus a one-line spoken tag ('Go away!'), with sensory and comic detail carried by concrete nouns.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: “Go away!” the puppet snaps.

claims.feature: background keywords in caps and bold
claims.claim: In the Background section, keywords are capitalized and bolded at first appearance to flag the adventure's important elements for the DM.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Keywords should be CAPITALIZED and BOLDED the FIRST time

claims.claim: Background must not bloat with backstory that is not ultimately important; the line between too little and too much exposition is explicit.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: doesn’t bloat the background with backstory that isn’t ultimately important

claims.claim: Each part of an adventure gets a one-to-two-sentence overview entry tied to a Story Objective.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: its own entry of one to two sentences describing the part

claims.feature: NPC block: 'What They Want' and 'NPC Snapshot'
claims.claim: NPCs get a physical/backstory paragraph, then two single-sentence inline entries: What They Want and an NPC Snapshot retitled to a two-word epithet.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: can be titled “Stoic Guardian”

claims.claim: Location text is organized under Area Information with inline subheads such as Dimensions and Terrain and Lighting.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Dimensions and Terrain.

claims.claim: Bold in running text is reserved for creatures and significant keyed objects such as traps and secret doors, used judiciously.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Use boldface judiciously.

claims.claim: Adventure sidebars give background that helps run a location and, except Playing the Pillars, avoid directly applicable rules content.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: shouldn’t provide directly applicable information

claims.claim: Encounters can carry a Combat / Exploration / Social triad of suggestions.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Playing the Pillars.

claims.claim: The 2023 AL template carries a CONTENT WARNING line on the cover and a Sensitivity Lead in the credits.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Sensitivity Lead: TBD

claims.claim: The adventure format defers to Chicago 17th and Merriam-Webster's Collegiate 11th for grammar and punctuation.
claims.source: DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04

claims.claim: The Word template defines the Boxed Text style solely for text a DM reads to the players.
claims.source: 1 - D&D AL Template.dotx (Jeremy Crawford, 2019-10) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: text that a DM is meant to read to the players

claims.claim: Epigraphs are not enclosed in quotation marks unless quoting a book that had them.
claims.source: 1 - D&D AL Template.dotx (Jeremy Crawford, 2019-10) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: An epigraph shouldn’t be enclosed in quotation marks

claims.claim: A sidebar that must immediately follow a passage is not a sidebar; integrate it into body copy.
claims.source: 1 - D&D AL Template.dotx (Jeremy Crawford, 2019-10) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: don’t make it a sidebar

claims.claim: WotC's content standards forbid profanity in D&D products absent special approval.
claims.source: DnD Standards (Wizards of the Coast, 2020) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Don’t use profanity.

claims.claim: D&D is described as mostly G-rated, sliding toward PG for mature themes or graphic violence; PG-13 products (Rick & Morty) need approval.
claims.source: DnD Standards (Wizards of the Coast, 2020) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: D&D is, for the most part, a G-rated game.

claims.claim: Standards forbid attaching traits to all members of a people, culture, religion, or sexuality.
claims.source: DnD Standards (Wizards of the Coast, 2020) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Don’t attach specific traits or attributes to all members

claims.claim: Villains may be sympathetic but their evil must be called out as wrong; evil heroes are avoided.
claims.source: DnD Standards (Wizards of the Coast, 2020) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: their evil should be called out as awful and wrong

claims.claim: Real-world religions may not serve as analogs for evil D&D religions.
claims.source: DnD Standards (Wizards of the Coast, 2020) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Don’t use real-world religions as analogs for evil religions

claims.claim: Perkins and Bilsland's second principle is that an adventure needs a credible threat with logical goals the heroes can uncover and thwart.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: An adventure needs a credible threat

claims.claim: Principle four: adventures are about the here and now; the less backstory needed to set things up, the better.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: An adventure is about the here and now.

claims.claim: Principle seven: present information as concisely as possible to ease the DM's burden, reserving descriptive texture for NPCs, dungeon dressing, and treasure.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: to ease the burden on the DM

claims.claim: Principle six: information appears in the order a first-time DM needs it, with an NPC introduced before being named casually and nothing important buried.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: An adventure needs to present information in a logical

claims.claim: NPCs get character through distinctive physical features, mannerisms, and quirks the DM can roleplay.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: features, mannerisms, and quirks

claims.claim: Familiar tropes (taverns, dragons, mad wizards) are acceptable if the adventure can still surprise; writers add their own spin.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: as long as the adventure can still surprise

claims.claim: The player characters are the heroes, not spectators; fetch quests for a lazy merchant are called out as underwhelming.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: The player characters (PCs) are the heroes

claims.claim: Text must account for players' decisions and alternate outcomes, or players feel railroaded.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: players will feel “railroaded” by the plot

claims.claim: Encounters are elevated by odd monster pairings, terrain, hazards, ruses, complex motives, and plot twists.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: An adventure needs to rise above the humdrum

claims.claim: The guide's craft advice is to read many good adventures, as novelists read novels.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: The more good D&D adventures you read, the

claims.claim: AL writers must not decide in advance how the adventure ends, even in a 2- or 4-hour slot.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: how the adventure should end

claims.feature: Chicago edition cited by the design guide
claims.claim: The design guide still cites Chicago 16th edition, one edition behind the style guide's 17th, showing the bundle's documents were not synchronized.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: Chicago Manual of Style (16th edition)

claims.claim: The design guide points writers to the House Style Guide for grammar and to the Adventure Format Template for layout, which is where boxed-text rules live.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)

claims.claim: The Forgotten Realms guide sets a hopeful tone in which the good guys eventually win, contrasted with cynical Greyhawk and tragic Dragonlance.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: The Forgotten Realms is a hopeful setting.

claims.claim: Stories must leave the Realms as found: no destroying or irrevocably changing established places, peoples, or gods without dispensation.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: (Pack it in. Pack it out.)

claims.claim: The guide instructs writers and artists to represent the Realms' many skin tones and ethnic analogs, including in cosmopolitan cities.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: Don’t Whitewash the Realms

claims.claim: Men and women are depicted equally in all roles; sexist clichés (damsel, sexy barmaid) are banned, with orcs and Northlanders as the two exceptions.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: Avoid clichés that reinforce sexist

claims.claim: Sex, romance, and gore are kept PG in Realms products.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: Keep it PG.

claims.claim: In-world characters speak of time loosely ('mid morning', 'nigh sunset') and, where clocks exist, in 'bells', not o'clock.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: “mid morning” or “nigh sunset.”

claims.claim: Days of the tenday are 'first day', 'second day', and so on; there is no weekend.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: “first day,” “second day,” “third day,”

claims.claim: The Realms guide bans a.m./p.m., coffee (kaeth), money (coin), restaurant (feasting hall), week (tenday), hourglass (sandglass), o'clock (bells), and generic subrace names.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: tenday (never week)

claims.claim: The Realms word list makes 'godsforsaken' the replacement for 'godforsaken'.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: godsforsaken (replaces Godforsaken)

claims.claim: 'Goodsir' is a lowercase form of address; Goodman/Goodwoman are usually capped titles.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: goodsir (a form of address, not capped)

claims.claim: Common is described as a pidgin trade language, less expressive than regional tongues, which may inform accents.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: Common is little more than a trade

claims.claim: The guide supplies stock greetings and farewells ('Well met', 'Until swords part') for in-world dialogue.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: Well met. The most often used greeting

claims.claim: The IP guide tells creators to stay experiential and not use exposition to explain the world.
claims.source: D&D IP Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: Stay experiential.

claims.claim: Monsters are mostly for killing and looting; non-combat monster roles are exceptions that need explanation.
claims.source: D&D IP Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: and their stuff is for taking

claims.feature: current AL requirement to follow the D&D Style Guide
claims.claim: The 2025 Dungeoncraft guide (v1.9c) requires the provided template and familiarity with the D&D Style Guide and DMsGuild content guidelines.
claims.source: D&D Adventurers League Dungeoncraft Design Guide v1.9c (effective May 2025, updated 2025-06-23)
claims.quote: You should be familiar with the D&D Style Guide

claims.claim: Dungeoncraft adventures must use the provided template, with an accessible non-template version permitted alongside.
claims.source: D&D Adventurers League Dungeoncraft Design Guide v1.9c (effective May 2025, updated 2025-06-23)
claims.quote: Adventures must use the template provided.

claims.claim: Adventures may not foster an atmosphere of competition between DM and players.
claims.source: D&D Adventurers League Dungeoncraft Design Guide v1.9c (effective May 2025, updated 2025-06-23)
claims.quote: atmosphere of competition between the DM and

claims.claim: The guide identifies itself as Version 1.9c, updated June 23, 2025.
claims.source: D&D Adventurers League Dungeoncraft Design Guide v1.9c (effective May 2025, updated 2025-06-23)
claims.quote: Version 1.9c (updated June 23, 2025)

claims.claim: The 2021 Witchlight Dungeoncraft guide already required familiarity with the D&D Style Guide, so the requirement has been constant across versions.
claims.source: D&D Adventurers League Dungeoncraft Design Guide: The Wild Beyond the Witchlight v1.2 (2021)

claims.claim: The 2024 rules capitalize conditions, actions, Hit Points, Armor Class, Proficiency Bonus, Long Rest and Short Rest as proper terms.
claims.source: D&D Free Rules (2024) Rules Glossary, D&D Beyond
claims.quote: Tags in Brackets.

claims.claim: In 2024 text a creature is any being including PCs, a monster is a DM-controlled creature, and an NPC is a monster with a personal name.
claims.source: D&D Free Rules (2024) Rules Glossary, D&D Beyond
claims.quote: a monster that has a personal name

claims.claim: The 2024 glossary speaks of creature types and species, avoiding 'race'.
claims.source: D&D Free Rules (2024) Rules Glossary, D&D Beyond
claims.quote: Most player characters are of the Humanoid type.

claims.claim: Jeremy Crawford confirmed on 2018-12-21 that the style guide permits singular they/them if the writer avoids ambiguity about antecedent.
claims.source: Sage Advice archive: "Have you discussed opening up use of they/their as singular pronouns in the D&D style guide?" (Jeremy Crawford, 2018-12-21)
claims.quote: careful about avoiding the common pitfalls

claims.feature: DMs Guild announcement of the 2019 update
claims.claim: The DMs Guild tweet of 2019-02-22 announcing the updated guide singled out its new gender-neutral language tips.
claims.source: Sage Advice archive: "Style Guide is now on DMsGuild, creators!" (2019-02-22)
claims.quote: tips on achieving gender neutral language

claims.feature: WotC's own term for read-aloud text
claims.claim: Crawford's 2016 poll names the device 'boxed text (aka read-aloud text)', the terminology WotC uses.
claims.source: Sage Advice archive: Jeremy Crawford poll (2016-11-17)
claims.quote: boxed text (aka read-aloud text)

claims.claim: Mike Shea argues brevity is critical and that living creatures should be kept out of boxed text because they may not be there when read.
claims.source: Sage Advice archive: "What are your thoughts on boxed text?" thread (April 2019)
claims.quote: Brevity is critically important

claims.feature: boxed text length ceiling (Greg Marks, AL admin)
claims.claim: AL administrator Greg Marks criticized boxed text that runs beyond a paragraph or so.
claims.source: Sage Advice archive: "What are your thoughts on boxed text?" thread (April 2019)
claims.quote: a paragraph or so

claims.claim: Shawn Merwin notes most DMs want boxed text, so publishers keep providing it despite streamed play rarely using it.
claims.source: Sage Advice archive: "What are your thoughts on boxed text?" thread (April 2019)
claims.quote: WANT boxed text

claims.claim: Merwin frames good boxed text as a series of prompts that convey atmosphere to the DM and push players toward action.
claims.source: Sage Advice archive: Shawn Merwin thread "This is exactly why boxed text is important" (2021-11)
claims.quote: excellent boxed text does a lot of heavy lifting

claims.claim: Justin Alexander names the freeze-frame pitfall: boxed text that advances the scene past the point where players could react, cured by actionable chunks.
claims.source: The Alexandrian, "GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls" (2022-08-01)
claims.quote: actionable chunks

claims.claim: Boxed text that declares what characters think, feel, or do removes player agency and is forbidden in Alexander's rules.
claims.source: The Alexandrian, "GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls" (2022-08-01)
claims.quote: you have effectively removed from the game

claims.claim: A commenter recalls a lost WotC developer blog from the 3.5/4e era saying boxed text should never exceed three sentences; the source is gone and WotC did not follow it consistently.
claims.source: The Alexandrian, comment by mellonbread (2022-08-02)
claims.quote: should never be longer than three sentences

claims.claim: The DMs Guild bundle (2018) comprises the IP guide, the adventure design guide, the style guide, and the Realms style guide, originally distributed to organized-play writers.
claims.source: EN World, "DMsGuild: D&D Style-Guides give a unique insight into the game" (2018-11-25)

claims.feature: WotC violates its own tenday rule
claims.claim: EN World readers noted WotC hardcovers still use 'week' despite the guides' tenday rule, reading the guides as newly formalized standards.
claims.source: EN World, "DMsGuild: D&D Style-Guides give a unique insight into the game" (2018-11-25)

claims.claim: The Realms guide's directive that characters should not travel to Sigil was read as WotC reserving Planescape for a future product.
claims.source: EN World, "DMsGuild: D&D Style-Guides give a unique insight into the game" (2018-11-25)
claims.quote: characters should not be traveling there

claims.feature: no public style guide update since 2019
claims.claim: As of 2025-06-13 a DMs Guild creator asked whether the style guide had been updated for the 2024 rules or Chicago 18th; the thread had no reply, confirming the public document is still the 2019 release.
claims.source: D&D Beyond forums, "Is there an update to the D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing document yet?" (2025-06-13)

claims.feature: where the current AL kit lives
claims.claim: The AL resources post (updated 2026-08-12) links the Dungeoncraft Creator Pack of 2023-12-04 on D&D Beyond's CDN while listing the Design Guide as 'coming soon'.
claims.source: D&D Beyond forums, "D&D Adventurers League Resources & Links (Updated 08/12/2026)"

claims.claim: EN World's 2023 report of the Planescape Dungeoncraft update states adventures must use official templates and comply with the D&D Style Guide and DMsGuild Content Guidelines or face removal.
claims.source: EN World, "D&D Adventurers League Unveils New DungeonCraft Document with Planescape In Focus" (2023-11)

claims.claim: WotC's 2020-06-18 statement committed to sensitivity readers on sourcebooks and to reviewing reprints for racially insensitive text.
claims.source: Gizmodo/io9, "Dungeons & Dragons Team Announces New Plans to Address Racism in the Game" (James Whitbrook, 2020-06-18)
claims.quote: That's just not right, and it's not something we believe in.

claims.claim: WotC said it worked with a Romani consultant to revise Curse of Strahd's Vistani text and named Tomb of Annihilation as needing similar updates.
claims.source: Gizmodo/io9, "Dungeons & Dragons Team Announces New Plans to Address Racism in the Game" (2020-06-18)

claims.claim: The statement said recent reprints of Tomb of Annihilation and Curse of Strahd already changed racially insensitive text, and each book would be reviewed at reprint.
claims.source: Wikipedia, "Tomb of Annihilation" (fetched 2026-09-06), quoting the 2020-06-17 WotC statement
claims.quote: we changed text that was racially insensitive

claims.claim: Ray Winninger said only the text of Curse of Strahd was revised; art and tarokka cards were unchanged and the revised text went free to prior D&D Beyond owners.
claims.source: Gizmodo/io9, "D&D's Culturally Sensitive Strahd Revamp Is Here, But It Doesn't Go Far Enough" (Julie Muncy, 2020-07-27)
claims.quote: surgical changes

claims.feature: Strahd Revamped: what the prose fix targeted
claims.claim: The revisions removed the depiction of Vistani as uncivilized heavy drinkers and softened an ableist portrayal, while leaving curse and Evil Eye abilities intact.
claims.source: Gizmodo/io9, Julie Muncy (2020-07-27)

claims.claim: WotC's announcement described the revamp as including the latest errata and a revised depiction of the Vistani.
claims.source: Wikipedia, "Curse of Strahd" (fetched 2026-09-06), citing PC Gamer 2020-07
claims.quote: a revised depiction of the Vistani

claims.feature: premise check: a public style guide exists, but not for boxed-text prose
claims.claim: The public WotC D&D Style Guide governs typography, terminology, and grammar only; WotC's only published boxed-text prose rules are the AL adventure-format document's sparing/one-or-two-sentence rule.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019') together with DC Adventure Format v1.3.docx (Claire Hoffman / Ma'at Crook, 2023-11) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
